new_statements.quote: All Cross River languages have systems of contrastive tone that co-occur and interact with intonational systems such as downdrift, register raising, boundary-related (demarcative) pitch-level modification, etc. Most have two levels of contrastive tone, but the Ogoni languages as well as some of the Upper Cross and Bendi languages have three level tonemes.

new_statements.relation_note: Snippet-stitched text of section 18.3 (each fragment returned by the Google Books feed today, overlapping): 'ACCENT, STRESS, AND TONE All Cross River languages have systems of contrastive tone that co-occur and interact with intonational systems such as downdrift, register raising, boundary-related (demarcative) pitch-level modification, etc. Most have two levels of contrastive tone, but the Ogoni languages as well as some of the Upper Cross and Bendi languages have three level tonemes. Gliding tones and phonemic downstepped high tones are common throughout the subbranch. At least some languages of every group for which instrumental or impressionistic data are available have different types…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every Cross River language (hence Ubaghara) is tonal with contrastive level tones, usually two (H/L), three in some Upper Cross/Bendi/Ogoni languages; downstepped H common; stress/accent where reported is phrasal (one peak per phonological phrase), not a word-stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Ogoni and some Upper Cross and Bendi languages have three level tonemes.
new_statements.identity_note: Family-level typological overview of Cross River (Bendi, Delta-Cross incl. Upper Cross); the statement is quantified over 'All Cross River languages', which includes Ubaghara (listed in the chapter's inventory as U4/U5 area 'Utuma ?.. Kohumono'), but Ubaghara is not discussed individually.
